title: Other views of the table
hookLine: Lutherans: Christ truly present in, with and under; Calvin: spiritual feeding; Zwingli: memorial

lines: THIS DO IN REMEMBRANCE OF ME.
cards: One table, one loaf, and a long argument about it. Paul says it happened on the night Jesus was betrayed.
In Luke's telling, Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, hands it round, and adds a request: "this do in remembrance of me."
Yesterday, Catholics and the Orthodox read his other words at that table, "Take, eat; this is my body." Today, three more chairs, each taking one small word in that sentence a different way. Is.

teach.b: Start with Martin Luther, who held on hard to that little word. Lutherans teach that Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine.
The bread stays bread, and Christ is really there, given into your hand. Lutherans don't explain how; they take the words as spoken. Then John Calvin, in Geneva.
Calvin taught that believers truly feed on Christ, but by the Holy Spirit, who lifts them up to him, rather than by Christ's body coming down into the bread. Real food, received by faith.
Reformed and Presbyterian churches stand in that line.
Then Huldrych Zwingli, in Zurich. Zwingli read is as signifies, the way someone points at a photo and says, that's my grandmother.

For him the meal is a memorial: the church remembers, gives thanks, and is joined together as one body. Baptist churches, among others, call the meal an ordinance: something Jesus commanded, done in remembrance.
But remembering, in Paul, is more than thinking back. Passing the words on to Corinth, he adds: "For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come."
Remembering is something the church does, out loud, together. And when Paul scolds Corinth about the supper, the first trouble he names isn't theory. Some go hungry while others eat first.
His fix is plain: "when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another." Wait for each other. These churches read the meal differently, and say so honestly.
None of their views lets anyone skip that verse.

how: Lutheran, Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist and other Protestant churches all keep the Lord's Supper, under names like communion or the Lord's Supper, and they explain Christ's presence in it in different ways.

games.q: what does “other views of the table” mean?
o: arguments over which bread to use at Mass
the seating rules at a church potluck
Protestant readings of the Lord's Supper

games.q: who said what about the table — tap the pairs.
p: in, with and under the bread
fed on Christ by the Spirit

s: Lutherans teach the bread is only a reminder
Lutherans teach Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine.
Calvin taught that believers truly feed on Christ
by the Holy Spirit, who lifts them up to him, received by faith.
Paul's complaint at Corinth included who ate first at the meal
some went hungry while others ate first. his fix: "tarry one for another."

games.q: you're Paul. word reaches you that at Corinth's suppers, some eat first and others go hungry. what do you tell them?
o: stop holding the supper until they sort it out.
when you come together to eat, wait for one another.
split into smaller groups of friends.
games.why: "when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another." whatever a church believes about the bread, this verse is about the people at the table.

practice: If there's bread nearby, pause before you eat and notice the many hands it came through: a field, a baker, a truck, a shelf.
If someone is with you, offer them some first and wait until they have it; if you're alone, bring to mind one person you'd want at your table.
If you pray, give thanks in words you already know; if you don't, let the pause itself be the thanks.

wordCard.voice: Other views of the table. Lutherans: Christ present in, with and under the bread. Calvin: feeding on Christ by the Spirit. Zwingli: a meal of remembrance.

orig.note: Greek: remembrance, the word in "this do in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19).

carryVoice: Your line: do this in memory. A table where everyone waits is as old as Corinth. Same time tomorrow.
